_International Women’s Day Issue_
**OVERVIEW**
At the beginning of 2024 — the ‘super election year — only 27 countries were led by women, showing a modest increase from 18 countries a decade ago.1 Despite this progress, women’s representation in political leadership remained critically low. Of the 31 direct presidential elections held globally in 2024, only five women were elected as Heads of State, representing Iceland, Mexico, Namibia, North Macedonia, and the Republic of Moldova.2 For Mexico, Namibia, and North Macedonia, these elections were historic, marking the election of their first-ever women presidents. Additionally, Mexico and the United Kingdom set an important precedent for inclusive governance by establishing gender-equal cabinets following their respective elections. At the end of 2024, the number of countries with female leaders had risen to 29.3
Despite these milestones, women continued to be significantly underrepresented in leadership roles. This persistent gap is driven by deep-rooted gender stereotypes, structural barriers and unequal access to opportunities within political institutions. In 2024, women accounted for just 23.3% of cabinet ministers globally—a meager increase of less than 0.5 percentage points from 2023.4 Even within this limited representation, women were predominantly assigned portfolios related to gender equality, social affairs, family, and children’s affairs, while strategic domains such as economic affairs, defense, justice, and home affairs remained male-dominated.

Legislated gender quotas emerged as a critical mechanism driving progress in women’s political representation.5 For instance, the Dominican Republic achieved an eight-point increase in women’s representation through stricter enforcement of quotas.6 In stark contrast, 12 out of 16 countries without such measures saw declines, highlighting the pivotal role quotas play in advancing gender equality in political leadership. Some critics argue that when gender attitudes intersect with ethnicity, implementing gender quotas to promote female politicians could inadvertently reduce the descriptive representation of traditionally disadvantaged ethnic groups.7 There are concerns that gender quotas may primarily benefit women from dominant classes, potentially pushing other minority groups out of politics.8 This has led to fears that introducing gender quotas could trigger demands for similar quotas from other marginalized communities seeking better representation in government.9 However, despite legislative gender quotas in many countries, the overall pace of progress was concerning. Notably, 2024 recorded the slowest growth in female parliamentary representation in two decades, with only a 0.03% increase.
As the global community aims to meet the Sustainable Development Goals by 2030, accelerating women’s participation in decision-making processes is not only a matter of fairness but also a strategic imperative for building resilient and inclusive governance systems.10
**What changed in 2024 — The Super Election Year**
In 2024, women’s representation in political leadership remained low, with **only five women elected as Heads of State out of 31 presidential elections worldwide**(through direct presidential elections).15 Iceland, Mexico, Namibia, North Macedonia, and the Republic of Moldova elected female leaders. Notably, Mexico, Namibia, and North Macedonia elected their first-ever women presidents, while Mexico and the UK set an example for gender equality by forming gender-equal cabinets.
Meanwhile, women’s representation in parliament remained stagnant at 27%.16 Among the 39 countries with available data, only 15 recorded an increase in the number of women elected, while 24 saw a decline. These trends highlight the persistent challenges to achieving gender parity in political leadership and legislative representation.
What changed in 2024 — The Super Election Year

In 2024, major elections took place in countries representing 3.6 billion people, yet the year marked the slowest growth (0.03%) in female representation in 20 years.18 Notably,27 newly elected parliaments now have fewer women than before, including in countries like the United States, Portugal, Pakistan, India, Indonesia, and South Africa.19 Additionally, for the first time in its history, the European Parliament also saw a decline in the number of women elected.20
**Towards Parity: Enhancing Representation with Quotas**
Although most countries have yet to achieve gender parity, gender quotas have played a significant role in advancing women’s representation over the years. In countries with legislated candidate quotas, women’s representation is notably higher—by five percentage points in parliaments and seven percentage points in local governments—compared to countries without such policies.
A growing number of countries are adopting gender quotas for public elections, with nearly half of the world’s nations now implementing some form of electoral quota in their parliaments.21 With the slow pace of growth in women’s political representation, there is a growing demand for more effective strategies to achieve gender balance in political institutions.22
There is strong and increasing evidence that women’s leadership enhances political decision-making processes. For instance, research on panchayats (local councils) in India found that areas with women-led councils had 62% more drinking water projects than those led by men.23 Similarly, in Norway, studies revealed a direct causal link between the presence of women in municipal councils and improved childcare coverage.24
Quotas are one such mechanism, offering a concrete policy approach with clear objectives and methods. Due to their relative effectiveness, quotas hold the promise of significantly boosting women’s representation in politics. However, despite their potential, quota systems also raise important questions and, in some cases, face strong resistance.
**CONCLUSION**
Women’s equal participation and leadership in political and public life are critical to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals by 2030.25 However, global data reveal that women remain underrepresented at all levels of decision-making, and true gender parity in political leadership is still a distant goal.26
**_Violence against women in public life_**

Violence against women in public life poses a significant threat to their participation and is a clear violation of human rights. As more women gain access to power, incidents of violence and harassment against them have seemingly increased.27 Women voters, candidates, and election administrators often face targeted, gender-based violence during elections.28 Gender-based abuse, cyberbullying, and sexual harassment targeting women in public life are becoming increasingly common online.29 Despite these alarming levels of violence, fewer than one-quarter of parliaments have a sexual harassment policy for parliamentarians, and fewer than half have such a policy for parliamentary staff.30
Ultimately, it is the responsibility of States to prevent, investigate, and punish acts of violence against women in public life, ensuring a safe and inclusive environment for all.31 This obligation is reinforced by international legal frameworks and agreements such as the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). There is an urgent need to intensify prevention and response efforts to address violence against women in public life. Key actions include reforming legislation, enhancing access to justice, and improving coordination among stakeholders. Critical steps involve criminalizing violence against women in politics, strengthening victim protection, building the capacity of state institutions and law enforcement to enforce laws and respond effectively to incidents, and bolstering judicial and complaint mechanisms.32 Additionally, it is essential to collect and monitor data on the incidence and prevalence of such violence and to establish clear standards for what constitutes online violence against women in public life. These standards would enable media outlets and social media platforms to be held accountable for harmful content.
**_Expanding Women’s Representation in Politics_**
Discriminatory social norms surrounding gender roles continue to hinder equal access to political participation.33 While attitudes toward women in public life have evolved slightly over the past 25 years, progress has been modest, even as more women take on leadership roles.34 In many countries, deep-rooted social norms and cultural values still perpetuate the belief that men are better suited for leadership than women.35
Achieving balanced political participation and equal power-sharing between women and men in decision-making is a key target established in the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action.36

**Dominica**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-16) officially the **Commonwealth of Dominica**,[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-17) is an island country in the Caribbean.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-English_constitution-18) It is part of the Windward Islands chain in the Lesser Antilles archipelago in the Caribbean Sea. The capital, Roseau, is located on the western side of the island. Dominica's closest neighbours are two constituent territories of the European Union, both overseas departments of France: Guadeloupe to the northwest and Martinique to the south-southeast. Dominica comprises a land area of 750 km 2 (290 sq mi), and the highest point is Morne Diablotins, at 1,448 m (4,751 ft) in elevation. The population was 71,293 at the 2011 census.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-2011_census-8)
The island was settled by the Arawak arriving from South America in the fifth century. The Kalinago displaced the Arawak by the 15th century. Christopher Columbus is said to have passed the island on Sunday, 3rd November 1493. It was later colonised by Europeans, predominantly by the French from 1690 to 1763. The French enslaved West Africans and transported them to Dominica to work on coffee plantations. Great Britain took possession in 1763 after the [Seven Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years'_War "Seven Years' War") and continued the legacy of forced labor to gain wealth, and gradually established English as its official language. The island gained independence as a republic in 1978.

Dominica has been nicknamed the "Nature Island of the Caribbean" for its natural environment.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-19) It is the youngest island in the Lesser Antilles, and is still being formed by Geothermal-Volcanic activity, as evidenced by the world's second-largest hot spring, called Boiling Lake. The island has lush mountainous rainforests and is the home of many rare plants, animals, and bird species. There are dry shrubland areas in some of the western coastal regions, but heavy rainfall occurs inland. The Sisserou Parrot, also known as the imperial amazon, is critically endangered and found only on Dominica. It is the island's national bird and is featured on the National flag, making Dominica one of the two sovereign nations whose official flag features the color purple.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-20)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-21) The country is a member of the Commonwealth of Nations, the United Nations, the Organization of American States, the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie, the Organisation of Eastern Caribbean States and the Non-Aligned Movement.
The Kalinago called the island _Wai'tu kubuli_, which means "Tall is her body", likely referring to the island personified as a goddess (comparable to Gaia).[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-22)

### Pre-colonial period and early European contact
With freedom came enfranchisement. In 1835, the first three men of African descent were elected to the legislative assembly of Dominica. Many slaves from the neighbouring French colonial islands of Guadeloupe and Martinique fled to Dominica. In 1838, Dominica became the first colony of the British West Indies to have an elected legislature controlled by an ethnic African majority. Most of these legislators had been free people of colour and smallholders or merchants before the abolition of slavery. Their economic and social views were different from the interests of the small, wealthy English planter class. Reacting to a perceived threat to their power, the planters lobbied for more direct British rule.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-bn-29)
In 1865, after much agitation and tension, the colonial office replaced the elective assembly with one made up of one-half members who were elected and one-half who were appointed. Planters, who were allied with colonial administrators, outmanoeuvred the elected legislators on many occasions. In 1871, Dominica became part of the British Leeward Islands. The political power of the elected assembly progressively eroded. Crown colony government was re-established in 1896.

Dominica stamps with portraits of King George VI and Queen Elizabeth II

### Pre-colonial period and early European contact
In World War I, many Dominicans, mainly the sons of small farmers, volunteered to fight in Europe for the British Empire. After the war, an upsurge of political consciousness throughout the Caribbean led to the formation of the Representative Government Association. Marshalling public frustration with the lack of a voice in the government of Dominica, this group won one-third of the popularly elected seats of the legislative assembly in 1924, and one-half in 1936. In 1940, administration of Dominica was transferred from the British Leeward Islands to the British Windward Islands.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-bn-29) During World War II, some Dominicans volunteered in British and Caribbean forces. Thousands of Free French refugees from Martinique and Guadeloupe escaped to Dominica from the Vichy-controlled French islands, staying in Roseau and other villages.
Until 1958, Dominica was governed as part of the British Windward Islands. Caribbean islands sought independence from 1958 to 1962, and Dominica became a province of the short-lived West Indies Federation in 1958.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-bn-29) After the federation dissolved in 1962, Dominica became an associated state of the United Kingdom in 1967, and formally took responsibility for its internal affairs.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23) On 3 November 1978, Dominica was granted independence as a republic, led by Prime Minister Patrick John.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-bn-29)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-48)

### Pre-colonial period and early European contact
In mid-1979, political discontent with founding prime minister Patrick John's administration climaxed in a civilian coup and ended in the passage of a motion of no confidence against John in the House of Assembly, Dominica's legislature, collapsing his administration. An Interim Government was formed under Dominica's second Prime Minister Oliver Seraphin;[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23) Seraphin's main task was to prepare the country for fresh general elections constitutionally due in 1980, hence the unofficial title "Interim Prime Minister". Seraphin organised and led a splinter of the Dominica Labour Party—the Democratic Labour Party—into the 1980 general election and lost mainly because his nearly 13 month-long premiership was dominated by the effects of Category Five Hurricane David, which caused 56 deaths and untold damage across the island.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-tcr3-49)Hurricane Allen the following year caused further damage.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23) After the 1980 election, Seraphin's government was replaced by one led by the Dominica Freedom Party (DFP) under Prime Minister Eugenia Charles; she was the Caribbean's first female prime minister.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-:0-50)

### Pre-colonial period and early European contact
In 1981, Charles's government was threatened with two attempted coups. The first was led by Frederick Newton, commander of the Military of Dominica, who organised an attack on the police headquarters in Roseau which resulted in the death of a police officer.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-coup-51) Newton and five other soldiers were found guilty in the attack and sentenced to death in 1983; the sentences of the five accomplices were later commuted to life in prison, but Newton was executed in 1986.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-coup-51) A second occurred later in the year when the country was threatened with a takeover by mercenaries,[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-52) led by Mike Perdue and Wolfgang Droege in Operation Red Dog. They tried to overthrow Charles as prime minister and reinstate ex-prime minister John in exchange for control over the country's development. The FBI was tipped off, and the ship hired to transport the mercenaries never left dock. The mercenaries lacked formal military experience or training, and most of the crew had been misled into joining by the ringleader Mike Perdue. White supremacistDon Black was jailed for his part in the attempted coup, which violated US neutrality laws.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-53)
Eugenia Charles, Prime Minister 1980–95, discussing the situation in Grenada in 1983 with US President Ronald Reagan
The Charles government supported the 1983 American invasion of Grenada, earning Dominica praise from the US government of Ronald Reagan, and an increase in financial aid.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-54)

Title: Mark Jason Dacua on Instagram: "November 3: Independence Day and Flag Day of Dominica 😊🇩🇲 It marks the exact date in 1978 when the nation achieved full political independence from Great Britain and officially raised its national flag for the very first time.

Dominica officially became an independent republic on November 3, 1978, ending centuries of colonial rule alternating between the French and the British. This historic milestone was led by the nation's first Prime Minister, Patrick Roland John, and President Sir Louis Cools-Lartigue. Historically, November 3 also aligns with the day Christopher Columbus first sighted the island on a Sunday in 1493, naming it after the Latin word for Sunday (Dominica).

On the very same day independence was gained, the original national flag, designed by prominent playwright and artist Dr. Alwin Bully, was officially hoisted for the first time at Windsor Park. This Cultural Division established Flag Day as an integral part of the month-long national independence season. It encourages citizens to honor their national identity, which is anchored heavily by the unique green flag featuring the endangered Sisserou parrot and ten stars representing the island's parishes. While the holiday honors the original 1978 flag raising, the revised version widely recognized today was formally accepted and finalized ten years later on November 3, 1988.

Today, this double occasion serves as the grand culmination of Dominica's vibrant Independence Season, filled with cultural parades, traditional Creole music, and nationwide displays of patriotism.

**Dominica**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-16) officially the **Commonwealth of Dominica**,[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-17) is an island country in the Caribbean.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-English_constitution-18) It is part of the Windward Islands chain in the Lesser Antilles archipelago in the Caribbean Sea. The capital, Roseau, is located on the western side of the island. Dominica's closest neighbours are two constituent territories of the European Union, both overseas departments of France: Guadeloupe to the northwest and Martinique to the south-southeast. Dominica comprises a land area of 750 km 2 (290 sq mi), and the highest point is Morne Diablotins, at 1,448 m (4,751 ft) in elevation. The population was 71,293 at the 2011 census.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-2011_census-8)
The island was settled by the Arawak arriving from South America in the fifth century. The Kalinago displaced the Arawak by the 15th century. Christopher Columbus is said to have passed the island on Sunday, 3rd November 1493. It was later colonised by Europeans, predominantly by the French from 1690 to 1763. The French enslaved West Africans and transported them to Dominica to work on coffee plantations. Great Britain took possession in 1763 after the [Seven Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years'_War "Seven Years' War") and continued the legacy of forced labor to gain wealth, and gradually established English as its official language. The island gained independence as a republic in 1978.

Dominica has been nicknamed the "Nature Island of the Caribbean" for its natural environment.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-19) It is the youngest island in the Lesser Antilles, and is still being formed by Geothermal-Volcanic activity, as evidenced by the world's second-largest hot spring, called Boiling Lake. The island has lush mountainous rainforests and is the home of many rare plants, animals, and bird species. There are dry shrubland areas in some of the western coastal regions, but heavy rainfall occurs inland. The Sisserou Parrot, also known as the imperial amazon, is critically endangered and found only on Dominica. It is the island's national bird and is featured on the National flag, making Dominica one of the two sovereign nations whose official flag features the color purple.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-20)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-21) The country is a member of the Commonwealth of Nations, the United Nations, the Organization of American States, the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie, the Organisation of Eastern Caribbean States and the Non-Aligned Movement.
The Kalinago called the island _Wai'tu kubuli_, which means "Tall is her body", likely referring to the island personified as a goddess (comparable to Gaia).[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-22)

### Pre-colonial period and early European contact
With freedom came enfranchisement. In 1835, the first three men of African descent were elected to the legislative assembly of Dominica. Many slaves from the neighbouring French colonial islands of Guadeloupe and Martinique fled to Dominica. In 1838, Dominica became the first colony of the British West Indies to have an elected legislature controlled by an ethnic African majority. Most of these legislators had been free people of colour and smallholders or merchants before the abolition of slavery. Their economic and social views were different from the interests of the small, wealthy English planter class. Reacting to a perceived threat to their power, the planters lobbied for more direct British rule.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-bn-29)
In 1865, after much agitation and tension, the colonial office replaced the elective assembly with one made up of one-half members who were elected and one-half who were appointed. Planters, who were allied with colonial administrators, outmanoeuvred the elected legislators on many occasions. In 1871, Dominica became part of the British Leeward Islands. The political power of the elected assembly progressively eroded. Crown colony government was re-established in 1896.

### Pre-colonial period and early European contact
In World War I, many Dominicans, mainly the sons of small farmers, volunteered to fight in Europe for the British Empire. After the war, an upsurge of political consciousness throughout the Caribbean led to the formation of the Representative Government Association. Marshalling public frustration with the lack of a voice in the government of Dominica, this group won one-third of the popularly elected seats of the legislative assembly in 1924, and one-half in 1936. In 1940, administration of Dominica was transferred from the British Leeward Islands to the British Windward Islands.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-bn-29) During World War II, some Dominicans volunteered in British and Caribbean forces. Thousands of Free French refugees from Martinique and Guadeloupe escaped to Dominica from the Vichy-controlled French islands, staying in Roseau and other villages.
Until 1958, Dominica was governed as part of the British Windward Islands. Caribbean islands sought independence from 1958 to 1962, and Dominica became a province of the short-lived West Indies Federation in 1958.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-bn-29) After the federation dissolved in 1962, Dominica became an associated state of the United Kingdom in 1967, and formally took responsibility for its internal affairs.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23) On 3 November 1978, Dominica was granted independence as a republic, led by Prime Minister Patrick John.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-bn-29)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-48)

### Pre-colonial period and early European contact
In mid-1979, political discontent with founding prime minister Patrick John's administration climaxed in a civilian coup and ended in the passage of a motion of no confidence against John in the House of Assembly, Dominica's legislature, collapsing his administration. An Interim Government was formed under Dominica's second Prime Minister Oliver Seraphin;[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23) Seraphin's main task was to prepare the country for fresh general elections constitutionally due in 1980, hence the unofficial title "Interim Prime Minister". Seraphin organised and led a splinter of the Dominica Labour Party—the Democratic Labour Party—into the 1980 general election and lost mainly because his nearly 13 month-long premiership was dominated by the effects of Category Five Hurricane David, which caused 56 deaths and untold damage across the island.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-tcr3-49)Hurricane Allen the following year caused further damage.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23) After the 1980 election, Seraphin's government was replaced by one led by the Dominica Freedom Party (DFP) under Prime Minister Eugenia Charles; she was the Caribbean's first female prime minister.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-:0-50)
texts.13:
### Pre-colonial period and early European contact
In 1981, Charles's government was threatened with two attempted coups. The first was led by Frederick Newton, commander of the Military of Dominica, who organised an attack on the police headquarters in Roseau which resulted in the death of a police officer.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-coup-51) Newton and five other soldiers were found guilty in the attack and sentenced to death in 1983; the sentences of the five accomplices were later commuted to life in prison, but Newton was executed in 1986.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-coup-51) A second occurred later in the year when the country was threatened with a takeover by mercenaries,[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-52) led by Mike Perdue and Wolfgang Droege in Operation Red Dog. They tried to overthrow Charles as prime minister and reinstate ex-prime minister John in exchange for control over the country's development. The FBI was tipped off, and the ship hired to transport the mercenaries never left dock. The mercenaries lacked formal military experience or training, and most of the crew had been misled into joining by the ringleader Mike Perdue. White supremacistDon Black was jailed for his part in the attempted coup, which violated US neutrality laws.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-53)
Eugenia Charles, Prime Minister 1980–95, discussing the situation in Grenada in 1983 with US President Ronald Reagan
The Charles government supported the 1983 American invasion of Grenada, earning Dominica praise from the US government of Ronald Reagan, and an increase in financial aid.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-54)

November 3: Independence Day and Flag Day of Dominica 😊🇩🇲 It marks the exact date in 1978 when the nation achieved full political independence from Great Britain and officially raised its national flag for the very first time.
Dominica officially became an independent republic on November 3, 1978, ending centuries of colonial rule alternating between the French and the British. This historic milestone was led by the nation's first Prime Minister, Patrick Roland John, and President Sir Louis Cools-Lartigue. Historically, November 3 also aligns with the day Christopher Columbus first sighted the island on a Sunday in 1493, naming it after the Latin word for Sunday (Dominica).
On the very same day independence was gained, the original national flag, designed by prominent playwright and artist Dr. Alwin Bully, was officially hoisted for the first time at Windsor Park. This Cultural Division established Flag Day as an integral part of the month-long national independence season. It encourages citizens to honor their national identity, which is anchored heavily by the unique green flag featuring the endangered Sisserou parrot and ten stars representing the island's parishes. While the holiday honors the original 1978 flag raising, the revised version widely recognized today was formally accepted and finalized ten years later on November 3, 1988.
Today, this double occasion serves as the grand culmination of Dominica's vibrant Independence Season, filled with cultural parades, traditional Creole music, and nationwide displays of patriotism.

**Dominica**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-16) officially the **Commonwealth of Dominica**,[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-17) is an island country in the Caribbean.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-English_constitution-18) It is part of the Windward Islands chain in the Lesser Antilles archipelago in the Caribbean Sea. The capital, Roseau, is located on the western side of the island. Dominica's closest neighbours are two constituent territories of the European Union, both overseas departments of France: Guadeloupe to the northwest and Martinique to the south-southeast. Dominica comprises a land area of 750 km 2 (290 sq mi), and the highest point is Morne Diablotins, at 1,448 m (4,751 ft) in elevation. The population was 71,293 at the 2011 census.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-2011_census-8)
The island was settled by the Arawak arriving from South America in the fifth century. The Kalinago displaced the Arawak by the 15th century. Christopher Columbus is said to have passed the island on Sunday, 3rd November 1493. It was later colonised by Europeans, predominantly by the French from 1690 to 1763. The French enslaved West Africans and transported them to Dominica to work on coffee plantations. Great Britain took possession in 1763 after the [Seven Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years'_War "Seven Years' War") and continued the legacy of forced labor to gain wealth, and gradually established English as its official language. The island gained independence as a republic in 1978.

Dominica has been nicknamed the "Nature Island of the Caribbean" for its natural environment.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-19) It is the youngest island in the Lesser Antilles, and is still being formed by Geothermal-Volcanic activity, as evidenced by the world's second-largest hot spring, called Boiling Lake. The island has lush mountainous rainforests and is the home of many rare plants, animals, and bird species. There are dry shrubland areas in some of the western coastal regions, but heavy rainfall occurs inland. The Sisserou Parrot, also known as the imperial amazon, is critically endangered and found only on Dominica. It is the island's national bird and is featured on the National flag, making Dominica one of the two sovereign nations whose official flag features the color purple.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-20)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-21) The country is a member of the Commonwealth of Nations, the United Nations, the Organization of American States, the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie, the Organisation of Eastern Caribbean States and the Non-Aligned Movement.
The Kalinago called the island _Wai'tu kubuli_, which means "Tall is her body", likely referring to the island personified as a goddess (comparable to Gaia).[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-22)

### Pre-colonial period and early European contact
With freedom came enfranchisement. In 1835, the first three men of African descent were elected to the legislative assembly of Dominica. Many slaves from the neighbouring French colonial islands of Guadeloupe and Martinique fled to Dominica. In 1838, Dominica became the first colony of the British West Indies to have an elected legislature controlled by an ethnic African majority. Most of these legislators had been free people of colour and smallholders or merchants before the abolition of slavery. Their economic and social views were different from the interests of the small, wealthy English planter class. Reacting to a perceived threat to their power, the planters lobbied for more direct British rule.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-bn-29)
In 1865, after much agitation and tension, the colonial office replaced the elective assembly with one made up of one-half members who were elected and one-half who were appointed. Planters, who were allied with colonial administrators, outmanoeuvred the elected legislators on many occasions. In 1871, Dominica became part of the British Leeward Islands. The political power of the elected assembly progressively eroded. Crown colony government was re-established in 1896.

### Pre-colonial period and early European contact
In World War I, many Dominicans, mainly the sons of small farmers, volunteered to fight in Europe for the British Empire. After the war, an upsurge of political consciousness throughout the Caribbean led to the formation of the Representative Government Association. Marshalling public frustration with the lack of a voice in the government of Dominica, this group won one-third of the popularly elected seats of the legislative assembly in 1924, and one-half in 1936. In 1940, administration of Dominica was transferred from the British Leeward Islands to the British Windward Islands.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-bn-29) During World War II, some Dominicans volunteered in British and Caribbean forces. Thousands of Free French refugees from Martinique and Guadeloupe escaped to Dominica from the Vichy-controlled French islands, staying in Roseau and other villages.
Until 1958, Dominica was governed as part of the British Windward Islands. Caribbean islands sought independence from 1958 to 1962, and Dominica became a province of the short-lived West Indies Federation in 1958.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-bn-29) After the federation dissolved in 1962, Dominica became an associated state of the United Kingdom in 1967, and formally took responsibility for its internal affairs.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23) On 3 November 1978, Dominica was granted independence as a republic, led by Prime Minister Patrick John.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-bn-29)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-48)

### Pre-colonial period and early European contact
In mid-1979, political discontent with founding prime minister Patrick John's administration climaxed in a civilian coup and ended in the passage of a motion of no confidence against John in the House of Assembly, Dominica's legislature, collapsing his administration. An Interim Government was formed under Dominica's second Prime Minister Oliver Seraphin;[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23) Seraphin's main task was to prepare the country for fresh general elections constitutionally due in 1980, hence the unofficial title "Interim Prime Minister". Seraphin organised and led a splinter of the Dominica Labour Party—the Democratic Labour Party—into the 1980 general election and lost mainly because his nearly 13 month-long premiership was dominated by the effects of Category Five Hurricane David, which caused 56 deaths and untold damage across the island.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-tcr3-49)Hurricane Allen the following year caused further damage.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23) After the 1980 election, Seraphin's government was replaced by one led by the Dominica Freedom Party (DFP) under Prime Minister Eugenia Charles; she was the Caribbean's first female prime minister.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica_-_Dominica-23)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-:0-50)

### Pre-colonial period and early European contact
In 1981, Charles's government was threatened with two attempted coups. The first was led by Frederick Newton, commander of the Military of Dominica, who organised an attack on the police headquarters in Roseau which resulted in the death of a police officer.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-coup-51) Newton and five other soldiers were found guilty in the attack and sentenced to death in 1983; the sentences of the five accomplices were later commuted to life in prison, but Newton was executed in 1986.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-coup-51) A second occurred later in the year when the country was threatened with a takeover by mercenaries,[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-52) led by Mike Perdue and Wolfgang Droege in Operation Red Dog. They tried to overthrow Charles as prime minister and reinstate ex-prime minister John in exchange for control over the country's development. The FBI was tipped off, and the ship hired to transport the mercenaries never left dock. The mercenaries lacked formal military experience or training, and most of the crew had been misled into joining by the ringleader Mike Perdue. White supremacistDon Black was jailed for his part in the attempted coup, which violated US neutrality laws.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-53)
Eugenia Charles, Prime Minister 1980–95, discussing the situation in Grenada in 1983 with US President Ronald Reagan
The Charles government supported the 1983 American invasion of Grenada, earning Dominica praise from the US government of Ronald Reagan, and an increase in financial aid.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominica#cite_note-54)
